newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court requires Britain to recognize working hours directive.
newsitem.headline: Court requires Britain to recognize working hours directive.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Tuesday the United Kingdom must recognize the working time directive adopted under qualified majority voting by the Council of the European Union.

Council directive 93/104/EC, commonly referred to as the working time directive, was adopted by the Council under article 118a of the EC Treaty. The directive limits weekly hours worked to 48, mandates four weeks of vacation per year and daily rest periods.
The root of the controversy before the court was whether limits on working hours could be adopted by the Council without unanimous approval. When the directive was adopted in 1993, Britain abstained.

The directive's legal basis is article 118a, which directs member states to encourage improvements in the working environment and tells them to harmonize rules on working conditions. Decisions adopted under 118a only require a qualified majority.

Britain argued legislation governing working hours should be adopted under article 100, relating to rights of employees, or article 235, a catch all article which can be used for issues not covered by the treaty. Both of those articles require unanimous acceptance of legislation by member states.
Arguing article 118a was to be applied narrowly, Britain characterized its language as an exception to treaty article 100 which deals with the rights and interests of "employed persons."

The court disagreed and noted that in its Opinion 2/91 of 19 March 1993, it said "article 118a confers upon the Community internal legislative competence in the area of social policy." Additionally, the court found article 118a is a specific rule relating "to measures concerning the protection of the health and saftey of workers," and not an exception to article 100.

The court said the existence of other provisions in the treaty do not have the effect of restricting the scope of article 118a, and noted that because article 118a is in the social provisions chapter and relates to protecting the health and safety of workers, it constitutes a more specific rule than article 100.

"It follows that, where the principal aim of the measure in question is the protection of the health and safety of workers, article 118a must be used, albeit such a measure may have ancillary effects on the establishment and functioning of the internal market," the court said.

Britain argued "working environment" relates only to the facilities and physical conditions at a workplace. But the court found no restriction in article 118a, instead finding the language "especially in the working environment" to favour a broad interpretation of powers conferred on the Council by the treaty.
The court noted the World Health Organization definition of health as a "complete physical, mental and social well-being that does not consist only in the absence of illness or infirmity."
Britain told the court the issue of how many hours employees work is not linked by any scientific evidence to issues of health and safety but the court rejected this outright.

The court also rejected Britain's argument that the treaty only allows the Council to put forward minimum requirements after looking at the conditions and technical rules in place by member states and was therefore a breach of the rules of proportionality. The court reasoned that "minimum requirements" language was included to allow member states to adopt more stringent measures if desired, not to set a low standard for workers.
Britain's arguments that the Council committed manifest error, misused its power, infringed essential procedural requirements and exceeded the bounds of its discretion were all rejected by the court.

The court did uphold Britain's complaint as to the second sentence of article 5 of the working time directive. "The court finds that the Council has failed to explain why Sunday, as a rest day, is more closely connected with the health and safety of workers than any other day of the week," it said.

application for the annulment of Council directive 93/104/EC of 23 November 1993 concerning certain aspects of the organization of working time (OJ 1993 L 307, p. 18) and, in the alternative, of article 4, the first and second sentences of article 5, article 6(2) and article 7 of that directive
THE COURT hereby
1. Annuls the second sentence of article 5 of Council directive 93/104/EC of 23 November 1993 concerning certain aspects of the organization of working time;
2. Dismisses the remainder of the application;
3. Orders the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland to pay the costs;
4. Orders the Kingdom of Belgium, the Kingdom of Spain and the Commission of the European Communities to bear their own costs.
